questions.lo: The particle model: arrangement, closeness and motion in solids, liquids and gases
questions.q: In which state are the particles packed closely together in a fixed, regular pattern and only vibrating about fixed positions?
questions.explain: In a solid the particles are held in a fixed, regular arrangement and can only vibrate in place, which is why a solid keeps its shape.

questions.lo: The particle model: arrangement, closeness and motion in solids, liquids and gases
questions.q: A substance flows and takes the shape of its container but cannot be squashed much and keeps the same volume. Which state is it in?
questions.explain: A liquid's particles are close together but can slide past each other, so it flows and takes the container's shape while keeping a fixed volume.

questions.lo: The particle model: arrangement, closeness and motion in solids, liquids and gases
questions.q: Why can a gas be squashed into a much smaller space, but a liquid cannot?
options: Because gas particles are smaller than liquid particles
Because there are large gaps between the widely-spaced gas particles
Because gas particles stop moving when squashed
Because a gas has no particles
questions.explain: Gas particles are far apart with large empty gaps between them, so they can be pushed closer together. A liquid's particles are already touching, so it can barely be compressed.

questions.lo: Density as mass per unit volume (density = mass ÷ volume)
questions.q: A metal cube has a mass of 200 g and a volume of 25 cm³. What is its density?

questions.lo: Density as mass per unit volume (density = mass ÷ volume)
questions.q: A block of wood has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 60 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explain: density = mass ÷ volume = 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 g/cm³, which is why wood (below 1 g/cm³) floats on water.

questions.lo: Density as mass per unit volume (density = mass ÷ volume)
questions.q: You have a 1 cm³ cube of iron and a 1 cm³ cube of polystyrene. The iron has far more mass. Which is more dense and why?
options: The polystyrene, because it takes up the same space
The iron, because it has more mass packed into the same volume
They are equally dense because the volumes are equal
You cannot compare density without measuring weight in newtons
questions.explain: For the same volume the iron has more mass, so density = mass ÷ volume is larger. Density is about how much mass is packed into a volume, not just how heavy something feels.

questions.lo: Changes of state as physical changes and conservation of mass
questions.q: Which change of state happens when a gas turns directly into a liquid?
questions.explain: Condensing is gas → liquid (for example steam condensing on a cold window). Evaporating and boiling are the reverse, liquid → gas.

questions.lo: Changes of state as physical changes and conservation of mass
questions.q: Why is melting ice into water described as a physical change?
options: Because a brand new substance is made
Because no new substance is made and it can be reversed by freezing
Because the mass increases when it melts
questions.explain: In a physical change no new substance forms and it can be reversed. Melted ice is still water (H₂O) and can be frozen back into ice.

questions.lo: Changes of state as physical changes and conservation of mass
questions.q: A sealed flask contains 60 g of ice. The ice melts completely into water. What is the mass of water in the sealed flask now?
questions.explain: Mass is conserved. The flask is sealed so no particles escape — the same particles are just rearranged, so the mass stays at 60 g.

questions.lo: The difference between heat and temperature
questions.q: At the level of particles, what does the temperature of a substance tell you?
options: The average speed (kinetic energy) of the particles
questions.explain: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy — how fast the particles are moving on average. Heat is the total thermal energy transferred.

questions.lo: The difference between heat and temperature
questions.q: A tiny spark at 900 °C barely warms your skin, but a large bath of warm water could transfer a lot of energy to you. Why can the cooler bath transfer more energy?
options: Because the bath has far more particles, so it stores much more thermal energy overall
Because heat flows from cold objects to hot objects
Because water cannot store any energy
questions.explain: Temperature is the average particle speed, but total heat energy also depends on how much matter there is. The bath contains far more particles, so it holds and can transfer much more thermal energy than the tiny spark.

questions.lo: The difference between heat and temperature
questions.q: When a hot drink is left in a cool room, in which direction is energy transferred by heating?
options: From the cool room to the hot drink
From the hot drink to the cool room, until they reach the same temperature
In no direction — energy stays put
questions.explain: Energy is always transferred by heating from the hotter object to the cooler one until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

questions.lo: Energy in matter: latent heat and changes of state
questions.q: On a heating curve, the temperature stays constant while a solid is melting even though the heater is still supplying energy. What is that energy being used for?
options: It is destroyed so the temperature cannot rise
It is used to break the forces holding the particles together, not to raise the temperature
It makes each particle grow bigger
questions.explain: During a change of state the energy (latent heat) is used to overcome the forces between particles and pull them apart, so the temperature stays the same until the change of state is complete.

questions.lo: Energy in matter: latent heat and changes of state
questions.q: What is meant by saying that boiling water requires 'latent heat'?
options: Energy is needed to change state without any change in temperature
The water gets hotter and hotter as it boils
No energy at all is needed to boil water
questions.explain: Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature — here it separates the liquid particles to form a gas.

questions.lo: Evidence for particles: diffusion and Brownian motion
questions.q: A drop of ink is placed in still water and slowly spreads out until the whole beaker is coloured, with no stirring. This is evidence that:
options: The ink and water particles are constantly moving and mixing on their own
Particles only move when you stir them
questions.explain: This spreading is diffusion. It happens because the particles are in constant random motion, mixing on their own — strong evidence that matter is made of moving particles.

questions.lo: Evidence for particles: diffusion and Brownian motion
questions.q: Under a microscope, tiny smoke grains are seen jiggling about in random, jerky paths. What is the best explanation for this Brownian motion?
options: Invisible, fast-moving air particles keep colliding with the grains from all sides
questions.explain: The visible smoke grains are being bombarded by much smaller, fast-moving air particles. This random bombardment is Brownian motion and is evidence that matter is made of moving particles.

questions.lo: The difference between mass and weight (W = m × g)
questions.q: Which statement correctly describes mass and weight?
options: Mass is measured in newtons; weight is measured in kilograms
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the pull of gravity on it (N)
Mass and weight are exactly the same thing
Weight never changes but mass changes with gravity
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms, and does not change. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass, measured in newtons, and depends on the gravitational field strength.

questions.lo: The difference between mass and weight (W = m × g)
questions.q: A bag has a mass of 5 kg. On Earth the gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. What is the weight of the bag on Earth?

questions.lo: The difference between mass and weight (W = m × g)
questions.q: An astronaut with a mass of 70 kg travels to the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is only about 1.6 N/kg. What happens to her mass and weight?
options: Both her mass and weight decrease
Her mass stays 70 kg, but her weight decreases
Her mass increases, her weight stays the same
Both stay exactly the same as on Earth
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of matter, so it stays 70 kg wherever she goes. Weight = mass × g, and g is smaller on the Moon, so her weight is much less than on Earth.
